sections.heading: Receiving every blessing from the Triune God
sections.text: Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, one God, you are the giver of every good thing I have now and every good thing I still hope for. Whatever blessing has reached me, it began with you. Whatever hope is still ahead of me, it rests in you.
theological_themes: God is one God in three persons, and every present gift and future hope comes from him as grace.

scripture_references.connection: James teaches that every good and perfect gift comes from God, grounding the prayer’s confession that all present blessings and future hopes have their source in him.
Paul’s blessing names the grace of Christ, the love of God, and the fellowship of the Holy Spirit together, supporting the prayer’s direct worship of the Triune God.

sections.heading: Only you can wake a dead heart
sections.text: You have taught me that hardship by itself cannot change my heart. Remembering my past sins cannot make me new. Even the honest warnings of people who love me cannot bring me to life. Unless you show me your grace and your Spirit works with power, my sinful heart stays dead. So I ask you to do what only you can do: make me alive to you, humble me, and turn me toward Christ.
theological_themes: Human beings are spiritually dead in sin apart from God’s grace; conviction, correction, and circumstances are not enough unless the Holy Spirit gives life.

scripture_references.connection: Paul describes sinners as dead in trespasses and then says God makes them alive by mercy and grace. This directly supports the prayer’s dependence on God, not circumstances or human persuasion, to awaken the heart.
Jesus says it is the Spirit who gives life, which grounds the prayer’s request for the Spirit’s powerful work rather than mere outward pressure.

sections.heading: Your love is deeper than my health
sections.text: You have shown me that knowing your love in my soul is not the same thing as feeling strong in my body. Physical health is a mercy, but it is not my deepest comfort. Sometimes, when my body is weakest and my outward life feels most fragile, you make your nearness and love feel especially real. Teach me not to measure your kindness only by how comfortable I am.
theological_themes: God’s spiritual comfort can be present and even especially strong in bodily weakness, so health is not the final measure of his love.

scripture_references.connection: Paul contrasts outward wasting away with inward renewal and teaches believers to look beyond visible affliction to eternal realities. This supports the prayer’s distinction between bodily weakness and spiritual comfort.

Christ tells Paul that his grace is sufficient and his power is made perfect in weakness. The passage illuminates the prayer’s claim that spiritual strength may be richest when physical well-being is lowest.

sections.heading: Teaching me to worship now and forever
sections.text: Thank you for giving me song as one of your gifts for my faith. Use worship to teach me, strengthen me, and lift my eyes to you. Help me take my small part now in the praise that never gets old—the worship already rising before your throne and before the Lamb, with angels and your perfected people.
theological_themes: Singing is a God-given means of worship and spiritual formation, and earthly praise anticipates the worship of heaven before God and the Lamb.

scripture_references.connection: Paul connects singing psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs with the word of Christ dwelling richly among believers. This supports the prayer’s view of song as a means by which God teaches and strengthens faith.
John’s vision shows angels and every creature worshiping the Lamb before the throne. This grounds the prayer’s longing to join the worship already offered in heaven.

sections.heading: Trusting your wise mix of sorrow and joy
sections.text: I bless you for not letting distress have the final word, and for not giving me joy in a way that would make me proud and careless. If sorrow were all I knew, I would be crushed. If ease and gladness were all I knew, I might forget my need of you. You are wise to give me a taste of both. Hold me steady in grief, keep me humble in joy, and make both serve your good work in me.
theological_themes: God wisely governs both affliction and comfort, using sorrow to humble and joy to sustain without letting either destroy the believer.

scripture_references.connection: Paul describes Christian life as sorrowful yet always rejoicing, showing that grief and joy can coexist under God’s sustaining grace.
James teaches that trials can produce steadfastness and maturity. This supports the prayer’s trust that distress, though painful, can be used wisely by God for spiritual good.

sections.heading: Longing for you as my life
sections.text: I love you for the little foretastes you give me along the hard road—like grapes in the wilderness, like drops of heavenly wine that make me long for the feast. Without you, I dry up quickly. Away from you, I am hungry, thirsty, and weak. But you yourself are what I need most. Help me keep holding tightly to your promise: you will never leave me or abandon me.
theological_themes: God gives foretastes of future joy that deepen longing for him; apart from him the soul cannot live, but his presence is the believer’s sufficient portion and assurance.

scripture_references.connection: Jesus teaches that apart from him his disciples can do nothing, grounding the prayer’s confession that life withers when separated from God.
David speaks of thirsting for God and finding God’s steadfast love better than life. This supports the prayer’s imagery of hunger, thirst, and God himself as the soul’s deepest need.
Hebrews applies God’s promise never to leave or forsake his people, directly grounding the prayer’s closing assurance in God’s pledged presence.

content_provenance.original_author: Unattributed Puritan source (compiled and edited by Arthur Bennett)
content_provenance.original_source: The Valley of Vision: A Collection of Puritan Prayers and Devotions, ed. Arthur Bennett (The Banner of Truth Trust)
content_provenance.source_copyright_status: Compilation, titles and arrangement in copyright (Banner of Truth, 1975); underlying Puritan sources are public domain.
content_provenance.modern_version_note: Contemporary prayer based on the theological themes and ideas of the historical source; not a reproduction of the original wording.

theological_issues_identified: The original assumes a strongly monergistic account of spiritual awakening: outward warnings, memories of sin, and suffering cannot change the sinner unless God effectually gives life by the Spirit. This is preserved without softening, though Christians from some traditions may frame human response differently.

The line about spiritual comfort being highest when bodily health is lowest could be misread as minimizing bodily suffering or implying that illness is spiritually superior. The adaptation keeps the contrast while clarifying that physical health is still a mercy and not the final measure of God’s kindness.

The original phrase “elect angels and saints made perfect” is biblical in substance but uncommon in contemporary prayer language. The adaptation renders it as “angels and your perfected people” to preserve the heavenly-worship idea without importing unnecessary technical language.
significant_interpretive_choices: “Remonstrances of friends” was interpreted as loving warnings or corrections from others, not mere criticism.
“Sensible effusions of divine love” was rendered as the experienced awareness of God’s love in the soul, rather than emotional intensity for its own sake.
“Clusters of grapes in the wilderness” and “drops of heavenly wine” were kept as concrete images of foretastes of future fullness, rather than flattened into generic encouragement.
